body:
A standard 8 x 8 x 16 in concrete block covers a wall at 1.125 blocks per square foot. Measure your wall, subtract openings, add waste, and you have your block count. This guide shows the formula, the mortar math, and how core fill works.

## The formula for concrete blocks

**Blocks needed = net wall area (sq ft) x 1.125, then add waste and round up.**

Net wall area is length x height, minus the area of each door and window. The 1.125 figure comes from the block face. A block face is 16 in x 8 in, which is 128 sq in. Divide 144 sq in in a square foot by 128 and you get 1.125.

The nominal size already includes a standard 3/8 in mortar joint. You do not add joint width on top. Block thickness, such as 6 in or 8 in or 12 in, changes weight and strength. It does not change the count, because the face size stays the same.

| Block face size | Blocks per sq ft |
| --- | --- |
| 8 x 16 in | 1.125 |
| 8 x 8 in (half block) | 2.25 |
| 4 x 16 in (half high) | 2.25 |

For mortar, Quikrete states that one 80 lb (36.2 kg) bag of Mortar Mix lays up to 37 standard bricks or 13 standard blocks. Divide your block count by 13 and round up for bags. Site mixed mortar from cement and sand uses a different yield, so check the bag you plan to buy.

## Worked example: a 24 x 8 ft wall with a door

Say you are building a shop wall 24 ft long and 8 ft high (7.3 x 2.4 m). It has one door opening 3 ft wide and 7 ft high. You use standard 8 x 8 x 16 in blocks.

- Step 1, gross wall area: 24 x 8 = 192 sq ft.
- Step 2, opening: 3 x 7 = 21 sq ft.
- Step 3, net wall area: 192 - 21 = 171 sq ft.
- Step 4, blocks before waste: 171 x 1.125 = 192.375 blocks.
- Step 5, add 10 percent waste: 192.375 x 1.10 = 211.6 blocks.
- Step 6, round up like a buyer: buy 212 blocks.

Check the math a second way. One course runs 24 ft, or 288 in. At 16 in per block, that is 18 blocks per course. The wall is 96 in high, or 12 courses. Gross count is 18 x 12 = 216 blocks. The door removes about 24 blocks of face area, which lands at the same 192 blocks before waste.

Mortar for this wall: 212 / 13 = 16.3 bags. Round up and buy 17 bags of 80 lb mortar mix.

Core fill, if your plans call for every core filled: Quikrete bulk data says one 3,000 lb bag of fine grout fills the cores of about 110 standard blocks. Here, 212 / 110 = 1.93, so round up to 2 bulk bags. Most walls fill only the cells with rebar in them, plus bond beams. Count only those cells if that is your design, and get the pattern from your plans or inspector.

## How do you measure a block wall?

Measure length and height in feet, wall by wall. Sketch each wall and mark every opening with its width and height. Multiply each opening and subtract the total from the gross area.

Keep your layout on the 8 in module where you can. Heights that land on full courses, such as 4 ft or 8 ft, cut waste and labor. Lengths that land on full or half blocks do the same at corners and openings.

If the wall steps down a slope, split it into rectangles. Work out each rectangle on its own, then add the counts. Our [square footage calculator](/blog/square-footage-calculator/) helps with odd shapes, and the [concrete calculator](/blog/concrete-calculator/) covers the footing that sits under the wall.

## What changes the block count?

Openings change it most. A standard door at 21 sq ft saves about 24 blocks. A garage opening at 8 x 7 ft saves about 63 blocks before waste.

Waste is next. Use 5 percent for a plain rectangle with few cuts. Use 10 percent for a wall with doors, windows, or corners. Use 15 percent for short walls, because one broken pallet hits a small order harder.

Bond beams, lintel blocks, and half blocks are separate line items. Your supplier can split a small part of the order into those units once you give them the opening sizes. Corners in running bond also use half blocks, so order a small stack even on a simple wall.

## Common mistakes to avoid

The big one is using actual block size, 7.625 x 15.625 in, in the math. That size leaves out the mortar joint and inflates the count. Use the nominal 8 x 16 in face and the 1.125 rate.

The second mistake is forgetting the footing and the first bed joint. The first course sits in a full bed of mortar on the footing, so it uses more mortar than later courses. Order one extra mortar bag on small jobs.

The third mistake is filling cores by guesswork. Filled cells add a lot of weight and cost. If the wall is structural, the fill pattern and rebar size come from code or an engineer, not from a rule of thumb. For a fence post footing instead, use our [post hole concrete calculator](/blog/post-hole-concrete-calculator/).

## Frequently asked questions

### How many concrete blocks are in 100 square feet?
At 1.125 blocks per square foot, 100 sq ft needs 112.5 blocks. Round up to 113 blocks, then add waste. With 10 percent waste you buy 125 blocks.

### How many mortar bags do I need for 100 blocks?
Quikrete rates one 80 lb bag at 13 standard blocks. So 100 / 13 = 7.7 bags, and you round up to 8 bags. Rough block or wide joints can push you to 9 bags.

### How much does a standard concrete block weigh?
A regular 8 x 8 x 16 in block weighs about 35 to 38 lb (16 to 17 kg). Lightweight versions weigh about 25 to 28 lb. A full pallet is heavy, so plan delivery to the wall line.

### Do I need to fill every core in a block wall?
No. Many non structural walls fill only cells with vertical rebar, often every 32 to 48 in, plus a bond beam on top. Structural and retaining walls follow a plan. Check your local code before you order grout.

### What is the difference between a cinder block and a concrete block?
Old cinder blocks used coal ash and are rarely made now. Blocks sold today are concrete masonry units, or CMU, made from cement, sand, and aggregate. The count math is the same. Our [brick calculator](/blog/brick-calculator/) covers the smaller units for a brick wall.
